The workflow starts automatically in two different situations. The first is when new code is pushed to the "main" branch which is the main project. Merging a pull request couints as a push so that triggers it too. The second one is when someone opens or updates a pull request asking th merge changes into "main." The pull requests are the only thing be tested. The deploy job has an "if" condition that lets it run only on a real push to "main" so the changes get checked but never go live until they are merged.
Step 1 is to checkout code which copies the project files onto the coputer running the workflow. Step 2 is validate the HTML which involves checking for mistakes like closing tags and using a standard HTML checker. Step 3 is checking links to make they lead somewhere. This step is set to a "continue-on-error: true" so broken links get reported but don't stop the process. Step 4 is upload the atifacts which is when the websites files get bundled into a package that's ready to publish. Splitting the workflow into two jobs keeps testing and deploying seperate. The "deploy" job uses "needs:build-and-test" so it waits for the first job to finish and only runs if it passes. The "upload artifiact" step is the excahnge between the two. It packages the tested files so the deploy job publishes exaclty what was validated.
GitHub runs every job on a brand-new virtual computer running Ubuntu Linux, and that computer starts out empty. The checkout code step uses a prebuilt tool to copy my project files onto it. Without this step the coputer would have nothing to check, test, or publish. Every step after it depends on those files being there.
The "environment" section tells GitHub where the site is being published. It labels the destination "github-pages" and fills in the site’s web address using the URL the deploy step produces steps.deployment.outputs.page_url." Each run is tied to that deployment and the live link shows up in the workflow and in the repository’s Deployments section. It works with the permissions section which allows the job pages to write. Those permissions are what actually allow the workflow to publish to GitHub Pages.
Deploying by hand means remembering every step each time and it's easy to skip one or upload the wrong files. This workflow runs the sames steps in the same order on a fresh copmuter everytime. Which also avoids "it works on my machine" issues. The key safety feature here is the "needs: build-and-test" which disables pushing until all tests pass so broken HTML never reach the live sit.
If I pushed to a different branch like "feature/profiles" the workflow would not run at all because it only watches "main." Nothing would be tested or published. The one exception would be if a branch has an open pull request into "main." My push updates the pull request then runs the build-and-test job to check the changes. But the deploy job is skipped because of its "if: condition." The live site only changes once code is actually merged into main.
